Carv.io – From time sheets to true capacity forecasting

Carv.io was born from a simple question most small and mid‑sized teams can't answer with their current tools: Are we staffed for the work that's really coming? Time trackers, ticket boards, and static resource calendars are good at recording the past and organizing the present, but they rarely help you see pipeline volatility, new skill demands, or the downstream impact of unexpected wins and delays. This case study outlines two working prototypes that push beyond record‑keeping toward simulation and prediction: a browser‑based pipeline simulator and a curved (Bezier) hours allocator.

The problem we set out to solve
SMEs need a planning approach that's fast to set up, cheap to run, and honest about uncertainty. They want to know whether today's people will cover tomorrow's work; how to cope with stressors like client slippage, internal hiring delays, or surprise sales; and where shortfalls or surpluses will emerge as projects enter, mature, or fall out of the pipeline. Existing tools don't model those dynamics—so we built ones that do.

Simulation framework v1.0 — modeling the pipeline
The simulation is a stand‑alone JavaScript app that runs entirely in the browser. It starts with a project template: up to five colored assignment blocks, each representing a role, arranged within a 26‑week window. Planners drag to reposition or resize blocks, capturing not just how much effort a role needs, but when it's needed. Every new deal that enters the pipeline clones this template, so patterns repeat consistently across many concurrent "project instances."

Capacity is explicit. For each active role, planners set full‑time equivalents (FTEs). The system converts FTEs to hours per week (1 FTE = 40 hours) and draws per‑role and total capacity lines. As FTE counts grow, the vertical scale expands automatically. A feed‑rate control governs how frequently new project instances appear from the right, so you can simulate slow trickles or rapid booking streaks.

Uncertainty is built in. Each project lives in one of four confidence zones—25%, 50%, 75%, 100%—based on where it sits along the sales‑to‑contract timeline. As time advances, projects cross boundaries; some progress, a proportion "dies off," and only the strongest reach 100%. Visual cues reinforce this: opacity tracks confidence (a 25% prospect renders at 25% opacity), and an optional ghost view compresses curves according to cumulative confidence, yielding a more realistic picture of probable workload rather than a best‑case pile‑up.

Results are live. The simulator continuously reports elapsed time, counts of past projects, totals in each confidence band, and role‑by‑role surplus/deficit against capacity. Because it's browser‑based, teams can explore scenarios quickly without standing up a backend.

Bezier allocation — shaping hours within a project
Capacity planning also hinges on how effort unfolds. Many tools assume flat distributions; real projects rarely behave that way. Our Bezier mini‑project lets planners shape a fixed budget of hours across a timeline using a quadratic Bezier curve driven by a single control point.

Drag the point to front‑load ramp‑up, peak midstream, or taper toward delivery—the system preserves total hours, pins start and end dates, and enforces sensible slopes (positive at the start, negative at the end) so curves remain realistic. A lightweight JSON model reads/writes the project's total budget, start/end week numbers, control‑point coordinates, and computed hours per week. Axes adjust on the fly: the horizontal scale labels "Week N" across year‑end rollovers; the vertical scale adapts to whatever weekly maximum the curve produces.

How it comes together
In practice, planners define a role pattern once, feed deals into the pipeline at a chosen rate, and watch as confidence‑weighted workloads rise and fall against declared capacity. When a particular project needs a non‑flat profile, they shape its curve with the Bezier editor—no spreadsheets, no manual re‑tabulation. The combination surfaces where and when pressure accumulates, which roles will be underwater, and what happens if sales velocity or kill‑rates change.

Why this is different

  • A systems‑theory lens. Instead of static calendars, Carv models flow—entry, attrition, maturation—and makes uncertainty visible.
  • Low‑resolution, high‑yield inputs. You can start with coarse budgets, durations, and FTE counts and only add detail when it materially improves decisions.
  • A foundation for recommendations. The simulator plus Bezier shaping provide scaffolding for a future engine that forecasts surpluses/shortfalls across multiple horizons.
  • Process‑agnostic by design. Whether your delivery resembles steps, waves, or something ad hoc, the framework can mirror it—and later ingest actuals from external time logs.
  • SME‑friendly. Running in the browser keeps cost and complexity low while still enabling meaningful scenario planning.

What's next
To move from prototype to product, we'll port the simulator into the Carv React app and back it with a Django/REST API for persistence and collaboration. Confidence modeling will get tunable kill‑rates, custom boundaries, and smarter arrival distributions. The Bezier editor will support multiple control points, editable start/end dates, and reusable curve templates (e.g., discovery‑heavy vs. implementation‑heavy). On top, we'll build a recommendation layer—statistical methods and ML informed by real time‑log data—to forecast staffing risk from one week out to six months. Finally, we'll invest in UX polish: richer visuals (heat maps, subtle animations), clearer ghost views, and mobile‑friendly interactions.

Outcome
These prototypes validate that a lightweight, simulation‑first approach can answer the staffing questions SMEs actually ask. By modeling the pipeline with confidence zones and letting planners sculpt per‑project effort realistically, Carv moves past retrospective tracking toward forward‑looking capacity management—the groundwork for a scalable, affordable portfolio planning system.

Prototyping a Hexagon‑based Puzzle Game: from Mobile App to Physical Board

Introduction
In late 2024 the design team behind Glassica embarked on a rapid prototyping journey to turn the idea of a hexagon‑based puzzle game into a working product. The goal was to explore how concentric hexagonal rings, colour‑mixing triangles and rotational mechanics could support puzzle modes for a single player and territory control for two players. This exploration progressed through three prototypes: an iOS puzzle app, a two‑player game built with p5.js and a physical board cut by laser. By iterating across digital and physical media, the team gained insight into how rotation, colour interactions and game state management translate between platforms.

1. iOS game prototype
Concept and mechanics
The initial prototype was an iOS puzzle game in which a player drags polyiamond shapes composed of equilateral triangles onto a concentric hexagonal grid. The board contains three rotating rings; the innermost ring has six cells while the outer rings have more. Key mechanics from the development milestones include:

  • Snap‑to‑grid placement – shapes can be dragged onto the grid and automatically align to the nearest valid position. The milestone plan required collision detection to ensure that shapes stay within boundaries and cannot overlap.
  • Colour mixing – the shapes come in three primary colours (red, blue and yellow). When a placed shape overlaps an existing triangle, the colours mix (e.g., red + blue → purple). Milestone 5 called for adding a UI control to set the grid's radius and applying colour‑mixing rules.
  • Rotating rings – players can rotate any ring by dragging. Rotation snaps to defined increments and allows clockwise and counter‑clockwise motion. Later milestones refined the rotation so that the direction depends on the quadrant of the drag.
  • Win states and scoring – when a ring rotation causes six complementary colours to form a full hexagon (orange, purple or green), the cells vanish and the player earns points. A score is shown at the top of the screen, and power‑ups such as undo and wild‑card pieces were planned to enrich gameplay.

User experience
Four screens from the prototype illustrate how these mechanics were presented to players. The main gameplay screen displays the concentric hexagonal grid with a preview of the next shape. The player's current level and score appear at the top, while icons on the right indicate available power‑ups. A snowflake icon freezes the rotation, and a rotation icon toggles between rotate and drag modes. Arrow buttons below the board allow the player to cycle through queued shapes, and a banner ad runs along the bottom.

A level‑selection screen shows categories such as Tutorial, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced and Premium with progress indicators. Within a category, the player sees a grid of puzzles represented by tri‑coloured shapes, and completed puzzles are marked with check icons. Finally, a settings menu offers options to return to the main menu, toggle sound, remove ads and reset progress. These screens demonstrate that the mobile prototype targeted casual puzzlers. Levels progress in difficulty, and the UI emphasises colour, rotation and scoring.

Strengths and limitations
The iOS prototype proved that the core mechanic of rotating concentric rings is engaging. Colour mixing adds a layer of strategy because the player must consider how primary colours overlap to form secondary colours and eventually disappear. However, it remained a single‑player experience and some of the planned features—such as three‑axis row/column dragging and elaborate power‑ups—were still in development. Testing also revealed that the complexity of managing numerous shapes could overwhelm players without clear tutorialisation.

2. Two‑player p5.js prototype
Goal and implementation
After validating the puzzle mechanics, the team wondered whether the core system could support a competitive game similar to the abstract strategy game Go. They built a prototype in p5.js, the open‑source JavaScript library for creative coding. The game runs in a browser and can be played in "demo" mode via a hosted link.

The two‑player game uses the same concentric hexagon board but divides the triangles between two colours—red and blue. Players alternate turns, placing their colour's triangles on empty spaces. Once placed, triangles cannot move individually; however, rotating an entire ring shifts all triangles on that ring, potentially breaking or creating connections. Capturing works similarly to Go: if a closed loop is formed around an opponent's pieces, those pieces are removed and score points. The game ends when all spaces are filled or neither player wishes to continue.

Notable design choices
In this version, the objective shifts from pattern‑matching to territory control. Shared rotation means that either player can rotate any ring; thus every decision affects both sides, and a well‑timed rotation can liberate one's own pieces or trap an opponent. The prototype uses minimal graphics to focus attention on strategy. It demonstrates that the rotational mechanic alone can support an emergent two‑player game.

Observations
Play‑testing showed that players quickly grasped how rotation changes the board state. The game encourages anticipating how rotations propagate across all triangles, similar to the way Go players think several moves ahead. The prototype also highlighted some ergonomic issues: with many triangles on screen, it can be hard to count liberties (open adjacent spaces) or see loops. These insights informed the design of the physical prototype.

3. Physical prototype via laser cutting
Fabrication process
To test the tactile feel of rotating hexagonal rings, the team designed a three‑ring board made from laser‑cut parts. Each ring consists of equilateral triangular cells connected to a central hub. Layers of acrylic or plywood separate the rings so they can rotate independently. Posts and spacers allow the red and blue rings to rotate independently above the yellow base, and the design required precise tolerances to ensure smooth rotation.

Manufacturing relied on Ponoko, an online platform for custom laser cutting. Ponoko offers on‑demand prototyping and production, with the ability to order a single part from as little as US$50 and get same‑day manufacturing and delivery. It provides cloud manufacturing technologies so startups can accelerate hardware builds. The service hosts over 200 materials and delivers parts with tight tolerances, removing the need for designers to research laser‑safe materials. These capabilities allowed the team to experiment rapidly: they uploaded vector files for the three hex rings and matching triangles, chose a material (e.g., acrylic), and received precision‑cut components within days.

Lessons from the physical prototype
Tactile feedback was a major benefit: rotating the rings physically gives players immediate haptic feedback. The friction between layers and the slight resistance when aligning to detents help players "feel" their moves in a way that a touch screen cannot replicate. Component tolerances matter—slight variations in laser‑cut dimensions can affect how smoothly the rings rotate. Material choice (e.g., acrylic vs. plywood) and spacer height influence the interplay between layers.

Translating digital rules into physical form also required adjustments. Some digital mechanics—such as instant snap‑to‑grid or colour mixing—are difficult to implement physically. In the physical game, players must manually align pieces and call out captures. This led to a simplified rule set focusing on territory capture and rotation.

Comparing prototypes
Although the three prototypes share the same concentric hexagon board, they explore different aspects of gameplay:

  • The mobile puzzle emphasises pattern creation through colour mixing and introduces players to rotation via power‑ups and level progression. It uses polyiamond shapes and snap‑to‑grid placement to create satisfying single‑player puzzles.
  • The p5.js version removes complex shapes and instead uses single‑triangle pieces for each player. Its goal is territory control, with shared ring rotation creating deep strategic interactions reminiscent of Go.
  • The physical prototype brings the mechanic into the real world. Players enjoy tactile rotation but must manually implement the rules. The design emphasises material choices and tolerances, influenced by Ponoko's precision laser‑cutting service.

These differences show that a single mechanic—rotating concentric hexagonal rings—can underpin both casual puzzles and competitive territory games, whether on a screen or a tabletop.

Reflection and next steps
The Glassica project illustrates how iterative prototyping across media can refine a game's mechanics and user experience. Starting with a feature‑rich mobile puzzle allowed the team to test colour mixing, rotation mechanics and progression systems. Building a simple two‑player prototype in p5.js confirmed that rotation and hexagonal adjacency can support deep strategic play. Finally, the laser‑cut physical board uncovered ergonomic considerations and enabled a social, face‑to‑face version of the game.

Future work could merge the strengths of each prototype. For example, the digital app could add a competitive mode inspired by the Go‑like prototype, while the physical game might incorporate markers or digital scoring to handle colour mixing. Case study: Web‑based music‑generation tools

Introduction
Generative music applications let musicians explore harmonic and melodic ideas directly in the browser. They commonly blend algorithmic composition, interactive interfaces, and—at times—machine learning to support composition and practice. This case study examines three modern web apps—Jazz Hero, Strudelizer, and Musical Call & Response—covering their goals, user experience, technical architecture, and opportunities for expansion.

1. Jazz Hero
Overview
Jazz Hero is a headless application with a Django REST API and an Angular front end. The flow is straightforward: choose or create a chord progression and root key, set filters such as approaches, line density, and song cycles, then generate a melodic line for practicing scales, approaches, and arpeggios. Registration is optional for exploration; an account is required to save progressions.

User interface and features
The generator provides separate sections for Treble and Bass lines. Users can:

  • Choose a chord progression via drop‑downs (e.g., blues forms), with support for adding custom progressions.
  • Select line density (eighth‑note or sixteenth‑note) to control rhythmic complexity.
  • Fine‑tune parameters using sliders for song length (cycles), rest density, octave range, note repetition, and approach repetition. An "Approaches" panel toggles various melodic motions (short descents, ascents/descents, "mini" variations, and arpeggios) to shape contour.
  • Set patterns and bass options mirroring the treble controls.
  • Generate and audition a new line, with options to listen and download MIDI.

Angular Material components power the sliders and menus, and the overall layout evokes a compact DAW‑style control surface that encourages experimentation.

Technology and architecture
Backend. A Django API exposes endpoints for progression management and line generation. The generator appears to rely on rule‑based phrase assembly and sample‑based playback rather than machine learning. The headless API is reusable for other clients.

Frontend. Angular (with Angular Material) renders controls and issues REST requests. A service worker may cache assets for limited offline use.

Workflow. Submitting the form POSTs the selected parameters to the API and returns either a MIDI file or a structured representation rendered via Web Audio or for download.

Evaluation
Strengths

  • Customizable generation. Rich parameterization (density, rests, approaches) supports focused practice on specific techniques.
  • Headless architecture. Clear separation simplifies reuse and potential mobile integration.
  • Practice‑first focus. The messaging emphasizes using generated lines for study rather than one‑click "improv."

Opportunities

  • Notated feedback. Adding staff or piano‑roll views with tempo‑adjustable playback would speed evaluation and learning.
  • Style breadth. Beyond jazz‑blues, support for modal, bebop, or arbitrary chord changes would broaden applicability.
  • Explainability. Tooltips and example phrases could clarify how each "approach" affects output.

2. Strudelizer
Overview
Strudelizer converts live MIDI input into Strudel (a live‑coding environment) syntax. Users play notes on a connected MIDI device or on‑screen keyboard and immediately see Strudel code that mirrors their performance.

User interface and features

  • Key & Scale controls. Users set tonic and choose from Western scales (e.g., pentatonic, major, natural/harmonic/melodic minor, diminished) and a range of Indian ragas (e.g., Bhairav, Bhairavi, Yaman), which drive both the keyboard and an XY pad.
  • Visual keyboard & XY pad. The keyboard reflects enabled notes; the XY pad captures controller gestures for expressive data.
  • Strudel MIDI Coder. Users select a MIDI device, clear captures, choose musical vs. integer notation, set sound presets, and adjust tempo and quantization resolution. A status area counts captured notes and shows the active device.
  • REPL integration. A code editor displays generated Strudel syntax with quick actions to copy or load into an online REPL. Keyboard shortcuts support play/stop.
  • Status displays. Panels report MIDI, audio, and general app status; utilities refresh or log devices.

Technology and architecture
Entirely client‑side JavaScript:

  • Web MIDI API for device detection and input capture.
  • CodeMirror for the editor/REPL interface, with Strudel's web REPL package for parsing/execution.
  • Modular structure (e.g., midi handling, coding, audio engine) for maintainability.

As the user plays, the MIDI handler translates notes into Strudel syntax (e.g., [c4, e4, g4]), applies quantization and tempo, and injects the result into the editor for immediate audition or reuse.

Evaluation
Strengths

  • Hardware‑to‑code bridge. Real‑time conversion lowers the barrier between instrumental performance and live coding.
  • Scale diversity. Inclusion of Indian ragas alongside Western modes invites cross‑cultural exploration.
  • Tight workflow. Integrated REPL enables instant playback and iteration.

Opportunities

  • UI simplification. Collapsible sections or inline help could reduce initial complexity.
  • Onboarding docs. Embedded guidance on Strudel syntax and typical patterns would help newcomers.
  • Immediate audio. A lightweight built‑in synth for the on‑screen keyboard/XY pad would meet expectations for instant feedback.

3. Musical Call & Response
Overview
Musical Call & Response combines interactive synthesis (Tone.js) with a Magenta MusicRNN back end to generate AI replies to user‑played "calls." Two input modes—keyboard and a circular, color‑coded wheel—let users craft a melody. The app then produces a response using a recurrent neural network (or, optionally, exact replica or reverse strategies). Scale systems span both Western modes and Indian ragas.

User interface and features

  • Scale selection. Users choose from major (Ionian), natural/harmonic/melodic minor, diminished, and several ragas (e.g., Bhairav, Bhairavi, Yaman, Kafi, Asavari, Todi, Purvi, Marwa, Khamaj, Kalyan). Selected scales activate allowed notes in the input interface.
  • Call input. A chromatic keyboard labels each key with note name and shortcut; a toggle reveals the circular interface, whose segments map to the scale tones. The call is visualized and can be copied.
  • Sound controls. Users select waveform (sine/square/saw/triangle), portamento, and volumes for a beat feedback synth and for an optional drone (with independent waveform).
  • Response controls. Choose Magenta (AI), Exact Replica, or Reverse; adjust number of steps, temperature (randomness), match/extend call length, and whether to clear or append after generation.
  • Generation flow. Status indicators show model loading and readiness; generation decodes the output sequence and plays it via Tone.js.

Technology and architecture

  • Client libraries. Tone.js for synthesis; @magenta/music for loading a pre‑trained MusicRNN (the commonly used "basic_rnn" checkpoint); D3.js for the circular wheel.
  • Scale logic. Arrays of semitone offsets define each scale/raga; selecting one filters the interactive UI accordingly.
  • Inference pipeline. The app records MIDI note values/durations for the call, then runs inference with user‑selected step length and temperature. Non‑AI modes bypass the model for deterministic replies.

Evaluation
Strengths

  • Cross‑cultural scales. Western modes and Indian ragas invite tonal exploration beyond familiar systems.
  • Creative control. Switching among AI, exact, and reverse responses—plus step/temperature—offers flexible practice and play.
  • Intuitive inputs. Keyboard and circular wheel suit different thinking styles; visualization aids review and copying.
  • Sound design. Waveform, portamento, drone, and beat feedback shape the character of calls and responses.

Opportunities

  • Model breadth. Offering alternative checkpoints (e.g., MelodyRNN variants or Music Transformer) could enrich phrasing and longer‑range structure.
  • Performance. Clear progress indicators and smarter caching would mitigate model load/generation latency.
  • Parameter clarity. Brief tooltips (e.g., explaining temperature and steps) would improve usability.

Conclusion
These three applications illustrate complementary approaches to web‑based generative music:

  • Jazz Hero emphasizes parameterized practice within jazz harmony, exposing the mechanics behind melodic shape and density.
  • Strudelizer links performance and live coding by translating playing into executable code, enabling instant remixing and algorithmic manipulation.
  • Musical Call & Response blends user control with AI creativity across Western and Indian scales, offering multiple response strategies and sound‑design options.

Collectively, they demonstrate how browser technologies can democratize music creation and learning. Future improvements—such as broader model options, richer visualizations and notation, clearer documentation, and performance optimizations—would further elevate accessibility and musical depth.

ChoozRoozy: Making Decisions Visible

The Problem We Faced
We've all been there—standing at a crossroads, our minds racing through countless factors, only to choose based on whatever thought happened to be loudest. Whether it's picking between job offers or deciding whether to go for a run, we often feel swept along by impulse rather than making deliberate choices.

This frustration sparked ChoozRoozy, a tool that transforms the invisible process of weighing options into something you can see and manipulate.

A Visual Approach to Choice
ChoozRoozy presents two options on a digital canvas—maybe "Go for a run" versus "Take a nap." Each decision factor becomes a draggable circle. Pull a circle left to favor one option, right for the other. Drag up to make it bigger when that factor feels crucial, down when it's minor. Red and blue circles show which option each factor supports, while purple indicates neutral factors.

The interface is deliberately simple. Users can rename options, customize factors, and toggle a "SHOW RESULT" line that summarizes the weighted outcome. An export feature captures decision snapshots for reference.

Transparent by Design
The underlying algorithm is intentionally straightforward. Each circle's position and size becomes a numerical weight. The system multiplies importance by directional pull, sums contributions, and displays the result. We kept the math transparent because our goal is prompting reflection, not mystifying outcomes.

Built with p5.js for its accessible, creative coding environment, the tool creates smooth interactions without technical overhead. Users remain in control—the algorithm reflects their priorities rather than imposing judgment.

Real Impact
Early users appreciate seeing how their priorities influence decisions. One described finally understanding their career change procrastination when fear appeared as an unexpectedly large factor. Another used it with their partner for financial decisions, finding the visual interface helped communicate priorities they'd struggled to articulate.

The tool became more than a decision aid—it helps people understand themselves.

What's Next
Future iterations could include saving decision scenarios, voice input for qualitative reasoning, different weighting models for complex preferences, and accessibility improvements to serve all users.

The Bigger Picture
ChoozRoozy isn't about algorithms—it's about reclaiming agency in decision-making. By turning abstract criteria into draggable circles, it helps users examine and refine their thinking rather than being victims of whatever thought happens to be loudest.

Sometimes the most powerful tools don't think for us, but help us think more clearly for ourselves.

Paragraphs Stats—Improving Component Governance in Drupal

Background
Knectar, a web‑development company based in Massachusetts, contributes to the open‑source Drupal ecosystem. One of the company's internal pain points was that clients often built Drupal sites using the Paragraphs module. Paragraphs allow editors to assemble flexible page layouts by choosing from predefined components (paragraph types). Over time, large sites accumulate dozens of paragraph types, and content teams frequently do not know which components are used, which are unused, or how extensively certain components are embedded across content types. Without visibility into usage, design improvements or clean‑up efforts are guesswork.

To address this problem, Knectar developed Paragraphs Stats, an open‑source Drupal module. According to the project's README, Paragraphs Stats is "designed to provide content managers and designers with a lens on how Paragraphs are being utilized on a given Drupal site." The module depends on the Paragraphs module and is installed like any other contributed module. Once enabled, administrators can access a new report via Reports → Paragraphs Stats Report.

Problem
When Knectar audited some of its long‑running client sites, it discovered that several projects had more than twenty different paragraph types. Content designers could not answer basic questions such as:

  • Which paragraph types are actually being used in the site, and how often?
  • Which content types contain specific paragraph types?
  • Are there unused or duplicate components that could be deprecated?
  • How can we confidently measure adoption of new components after a redesign?

Without answers, teams hesitated to remove unused components or to refactor because they feared breaking pages. The existing Paragraphs module does not provide reporting features, so site builders had to write ad‑hoc SQL queries or rely on guesses.

Solution – Paragraphs Stats
Feature overview
Paragraphs Stats adds a reporting interface to Drupal that summarizes paragraph usage across the entire site. The module registers a Paragraphs Stats Report link under the Reports menu and defines user permissions so that only authorized roles can view or configure the report. The module's routing file shows that it exposes several paths:

  • A main report at /admin/reports/paragraphs-stats-report which displays the high‑level utilization matrix.
  • Drill‑down reports that show which nodes, custom block types or paragraph entities contain a particular component.
  • A path to update the internal metadata (/update-structure) requiring an administrative permission. This job scans all entity bundles and fields, populating a metadata table that tracks which paragraph types can be used where.
  • An export path (/export/csv) that triggers a CSV download.

These routes are controlled by PsController, which simply delegates requests to a service class (ParagraphsStats) that builds the reports.

Building the utilization matrix
The heart of the module is the utilization report, a matrix showing every paragraph type down the left side and every enabled content type (or block/paragraph entity) across the top. The getUtilizationTabularData() method in the ParagraphsStats service constructs this data structure. It begins by adding two header columns—"Paragraph" and "Paragraph machine name." For each content type configured for reporting, it appends a column header that contains the content‑type label, machine name and a count of how many entities of that type exist; each header links to Drupal's content listing page for that type.

The method then executes a query to count how many times each paragraph appears in each content type and calculates a usage level for each count. Usage levels map to numeric classes (v-0 through v-4) that correspond to color ranges defined in the module's CSS file: heavily used cells have shades of green and under‑used ones have red tones. For each paragraph type and content type, the module inserts either a clickable number that links to a drill‑down report or a placeholder (0 or n/a) when the paragraph is unused or not applicable. The main report also includes a legend explaining that n/a indicates that a paragraph type is not available for the content type.

Drill‑down and usage reports
When a user clicks on a count in the matrix, they are taken to a drill‑down report. The showUtilizationDrillDown() controller method sanitizes the parameters and invokes getDrillDownTable(). This method queries the database to find individual host entities (nodes, block_content or paragraph entities) that contain the selected component. The drill‑down report lists the URL of each host entity, the field where the paragraph appears, the number of times it occurs and an action link (e.g., editing the node or viewing a further usage report). The rows are tallied, and a "TOTAL" row provides a sum at the bottom.

Paragraphs Stats also provides a Paragraph usage report for a specific paragraph entity. The showParagraphUsage() method assembles a table showing where a particular paragraph instance is reused (e.g., within nodes, blocks or other paragraphs) and counts each occurrence. This helps editors understand whether changing or deleting a paragraph will impact other content.

Updating the metadata and exporting
Paragraphs Stats relies on its own metadata table to know which paragraph types are allowed in each entity bundle. Administrators run the Update structure action from the report UI, which calls the updateStructure() method. This method scans every entity type and bundle, inspects each field definition, and records the allowed paragraph types into a database table. The update process returns a simple message with a link back to the main report. Without this step, new paragraph types added after initial installation would not appear in the report.

For further analysis, the Export to CSV button calls exportCsv(), which packages the tabular data into a downloadable CSV file and names it with a timestamp. The module uses Drupal's Link and Symfony's Response classes to generate the download.

Implementation at Kettering University
Kettering University's marketing team needed to streamline the school's Drupal 9 website before a major redesign. Over five years, editors had created dozens of custom paragraph types to experiment with page designs. Many components served similar purposes—such as call‑to‑action banners or testimonial blocks—but it was unclear which ones were actively used.

Knectar installed Paragraphs Stats and configured it to scan Kettering's main node types (programs, departments, co‑op experience pages) as well as custom block types. Running the update process populated the metadata table and generated the utilization matrix. The team quickly saw that only around half of the existing components were still used. For example, a row labeled "Banner CTA" had high counts for program pages and admissions pages, while "Feature Icon Row" had zero usage across all content types. Red cells highlighted seldom‑used components. By drilling down, the team identified the handful of pages that still contained older components and migrated those pages to newer designs.

During the redesign, content designers used the report to measure adoption of new components. After releasing a new "Student Story" paragraph, they observed that it was used on more than 70% of program pages within two months. This data justified prioritizing further enhancements to that component. Exporting the matrix to CSV allowed the marketing team to share the analysis with stakeholders and track progress over time.

Impact
Implementing Paragraphs Stats delivered several benefits for Kettering University and Knectar's broader client base:

  • Improved governance: The utilization matrix provided clear evidence of unused or redundant components, enabling the team to retire 12 outdated paragraph types without fear of breaking pages. This simplified the editor UI and reduced maintenance overhead.
  • Data‑driven redesign: Designers could see which components were heavily used, guiding them to focus enhancements on the most impactful elements. Tracking adoption of new components also validated design decisions.
  • Performance and stability: Removing unused components reduced code complexity and database queries, which contributed to faster page loads and easier upgrades to Drupal 10.
  • Reusability across projects: Because Paragraphs Stats is open source, Knectar integrated it into other client projects to facilitate periodic audits of component usage.

Conclusion and future enhancements
Paragraphs Stats fills a gap in Drupal's Paragraphs ecosystem by giving content teams a visual and actionable understanding of how components are used across their sites. The module's installation is straightforward, and its reports—complete with drill‑downs, color‑coded usage levels and CSV export—empower site administrators to make data‑driven decisions about component libraries. Kettering University's experience shows how such insights can lead to leaner, more maintainable websites and more effective redesigns.

Future enhancements under consideration include scheduling automatic metadata updates, integrating with Google Analytics to correlate component usage with page performance, and adding support for paragraph variations defined through the Layout Builder. By releasing Paragraphs Stats to the Drupal community and maintaining it alongside core upgrades, Knectar demonstrates how a targeted open‑source contribution can improve content governance for a wide range of sites.

Client background

Monadnock Media is an independent media organization serving the Monadnock region of New Hampshire with community-focused journalism. Founded in 2019, the organization publishes Monadnock Ledger-Transcript, a weekly newspaper covering local news, events and issues in the region. The team includes experienced journalists and editors committed to providing quality local journalism that serves the community's information needs.

Project goals and challenges

Monadnock Media needed a modern, flexible website that could support their journalism mission while providing an excellent user experience for readers. The team identified several key goals:

  • Create a headless CMS architecture. Build a Strapi-based content management system that would provide a robust backend for managing articles, authors, categories and multimedia content while enabling flexible front-end development.
  • Develop an engaging front-end experience. Work with design partner Aaron Taylor-Waldman to create a modern, responsive website that would showcase journalism effectively and provide an intuitive reading experience across devices.
  • Support advanced front-end development. Implement sophisticated animations, scroll-triggered effects and interactive elements that would enhance storytelling without compromising performance or accessibility.
  • Enable content management workflows. Provide editors and journalists with an intuitive interface for creating, editing and publishing content while maintaining editorial standards and brand consistency.

Approach

Headless CMS architecture with Strapi

The project began with implementing a Strapi headless CMS as the content management foundation. Strapi provided a flexible, API-first approach that would allow for sophisticated content modeling while enabling the front-end team to work independently. The CMS was configured with content types for articles, authors, categories, tags and multimedia assets, with custom fields and relationships to support the newspaper's editorial workflow.

Front-end development and animation prototyping

Knectar handled the front-end development, working closely with Aaron Taylor-Waldman's design vision to create a modern, engaging website. The development focused on advanced front-end techniques including scroll-triggered animations, quasi-3D layering effects and interactive elements that would enhance the reading experience. The team experimented with WebGL and p5.js for creating tactile, fluid interactions that would make the site feel more engaging and modern.

Scroll-triggered effects and interaction architecture

A key focus was implementing sophisticated scroll-triggered effects that would enhance storytelling without being distracting. This included techniques like scroll-triggered video/animation playback, parallax effects and dynamic content reveals that would engage readers as they moved through articles. The team used Svelte for implementing scroll triggers and other interactive elements, taking advantage of the framework's performance and developer experience.

Content management and editorial workflows

The Strapi CMS was configured to support the newspaper's editorial workflow, with user roles and permissions that matched the organization's structure. Editors could manage content through an intuitive interface, with features for scheduling publications, managing drafts and coordinating with the design team. The system also included tools for managing multimedia content, ensuring that images, videos and other assets were properly optimized and integrated into articles.

Performance optimization and responsive design

Performance was a critical consideration throughout development. The team implemented lazy loading for images and videos, optimized CSS and JavaScript delivery, and ensured that the site would load quickly across different devices and connection speeds. The responsive design was tested across various screen sizes to ensure an optimal reading experience for mobile, tablet and desktop users.

Outcomes

The new Monadnock Media website delivered a modern, engaging platform that successfully supported the organization's journalism mission. The headless CMS architecture provided the flexibility needed for both content management and front-end development, while the sophisticated animations and interactive elements created a more engaging reading experience that helped distinguish the publication in the competitive local media landscape.

The scroll-triggered effects and quasi-3D layering added visual interest without compromising the readability of articles, and the responsive design ensured that readers could access content effectively across all devices. The Strapi CMS streamlined editorial workflows, making it easier for journalists and editors to manage content while maintaining the publication's high editorial standards.

In summary

The Monadnock Media project demonstrated the value of combining a robust headless CMS with advanced front-end development techniques. By using Strapi for content management and implementing sophisticated animations and interactions, the team created a website that not only served the practical needs of a local newspaper but also provided an engaging, modern user experience that helped the publication stand out in the digital media landscape.

submenu.label: Robert Rauschenberg Foundation
submenu.projectTitle: Robert Rauschenberg Foundation: Drupal 7 to 10 Website Migration
submenu.project_haiku:
Art lives beyond time
Digital archives preserve
Creative spirit soars
submenu.project_footer_CTA: Ready to preserve and celebrate artistic legacy through digital innovation? Let's create something timeless.
submenu.pageSummary:
Client background

The Robert Rauschenberg Foundation (RRF) is a non‑profit founded by the artist Robert Rauschenberg in 1990. A pioneering figure in post‑war art, Rauschenberg served in the U.S. Navy before studying at the Kansas City Art Institute, the Académie Julian in Paris and Black Mountain College, and he moved to New York in 1949 where he challenged artistic conventions with his Combinesrauschenbergfoundation.org. Today the Foundation builds on his legacy and emphasizes his belief that artists can drive social changerauschenbergfoundation.org. The organization supports programs and residencies and stewards an extensive archive that preserves the most comprehensive body of information on Rauschenberg's life and careerrauschenbergfoundation.org, making it both a cultural authority and a philanthropic institution of international prestigerauschenbergfoundation.org.

Project goals and challenges

By 2024 the Foundation's public website had grown into a complex Drupal 7 platform with dozens of content types and views. Non‑technical staff found it difficult to manage because many pages were entirely built using Views and custom templates. The site hosted more than a thousand artwork records, hundreds of archive entries and a wide range of program pages and timelines, much of which was entered through a FileMaker database. The team identified several key goals:

  • Modernize the CMS. Move from Drupal 7 to Drupal 10 to ensure long‑term support, improve security and leverage modern editing tools.
  • Simplify content management. Consolidate multiple basic‑page content types and heavy Views into a smaller set of flexible blocks so that non‑developers could update pages via Drupal 10's Layout Builder.
  • Integrate the FileMaker database. Use the Feeds FileMaker Module to import artwork and archive records. The existing FileMaker integration raised questions about whether artwork nodes should remain editable in Drupal or only in FileMaker and which fields could be eliminated.
  • Improve user experience. Preserve the ability to filter and search artworks and archives while streamlining navigation. Migrate specialized pages—such as the chronology, exhibition history and lightboxes—and consider richer visualizations such as an interactive timeline.
  • Consolidate mapping pages. On View and Public Collections pages both displayed works on maps via Pin Collection nodes; the new site needed to combine them into a single map with filterable pins while retaining the lists underneath.

Approach

Architecture and content strategy

A comprehensive content audit catalogued all Drupal 7 content types, views and templates. The audit recommended manually migrating simple pages and scripting the migration of large datasets such as artworks, series and archive entries. Content types such as Basic Page Centered, Basic Page Left Justified and Landing Page were consolidated into a single Basic Page to reduce complexity. The team also proposed using tile blocks and featured blocks to replace ad‑hoc views and create a consistent visual language for programs and collaborations pages.

Drupal 10 and Layout Builder

Drupal 10's Layout Builder gave non‑technical editors control over page composition. On the new home page, hero images, captions and introductory text became editable blocks instead of being buried in views. News items remained automatically generated by date but were exposed as a block that editors could reorder. The artwork, artist and programs sections were similarly transformed into layout‑builder sections, making the old Homepage Sections content type obsolete.

FileMaker integration via Feeds

Artwork and archive records originated from the Foundation's FileMaker database. To avoid manual data entry, the team used the Feeds FileMaker Module to connect Drupal 10 to the FileMaker PHP API, retrieve records and map fields to Drupal entities. The migration plan raised critical questions about which fields to retain and whether to allow edits in Drupal or force changes in FileMaker. The solution was to import core descriptive metadata (titles, dates, medium, credit lines) from FileMaker while adding a small number of Drupal‑only fields for features like exhibitions or notes that curators wanted to edit directly. Feeds setups were configured to run automatically on a schedule, ensuring that new or updated artworks and archives appeared on the site without manual intervention. A similar approach was taken for Series and Lightbox entities, allowing future automation based on FileMaker's series field.

Search, filtering and mapping

The artwork and archive search pages remained Views because they needed sophisticated filtering by medium, year and category. Drupal 10's Search API and Facets modules were used to replace older custom search code. For the On View and Public Collections pages, the team combined the two maps into a single map component with filterable pins; different colors indicated whether a work was currently on view or part of a public collection.

Chronology and exhibition history

The existing chronology page concatenated Chronology Section nodes into a long two‑column list, which was cumbersome for visitors and editors. The team evaluated modules like Views TimelineJS and external services such as Knight Lab's Timeline to build an interactive timeline that allows visitors to scroll through key events and search within the timeline. Exhibition history and performance history pages, previously built as Book Pages, were converted to Basic Pages with tertiary navigation items for easier management.

Programs and residencies

Program and residency pages were turned into Basic Pages with reusable blurb blocks. For example, the residencies landing page originally built with a Landing Page content type became a basic page where editors could add blurbs highlighting the Rauschenberg Residency on Captiva, the Archives Research Residency and the Rauschenberg Residency 381. Subpages like the chef‑in‑residence program and site history were migrated manually and organized using secondary navigation.

Outcomes

The new site delivered a streamlined editing experience and a more engaging presentation of the Foundation's collections and programs. Editors now manage hero images, news blocks and feature tiles through an intuitive drag‑and‑drop interface, eliminating the need to edit complex views. Automated imports from FileMaker ensure that the art and archive sections remain up to date without manual intervention. Consolidating content types and simplifying navigation reduce maintenance overhead and make it easier for users to find information. The combined On View/Public Collections map offers visitors a single point of entry to discover where Rauschenberg's works are exhibited worldwide, while the planned interactive timeline will bring his chronology to life. By migrating to Drupal 10 and leveraging modern modules like Feeds, Layout Builder and Search API, the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation has positioned its website to support its mission—promoting Rauschenberg's artistic and philanthropic legacyrauschenbergfoundation.org—for years to come.

In summary

In summary, the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation's move from Drupal 7 to Drupal 10 aimed to simplify content management, improve performance, and integrate a FileMaker database using the Feeds FileMaker module. The team consolidated numerous legacy content types into a single Basic Page format and adopted Layout Builder to empower non-developers with drag-and-drop page construction. Complex Views were retained only where advanced filtering was essential, such as for the searchable artwork and archive sections.

The integration with FileMaker automates the import of art and archive records while allowing select fields to be editable in Drupal, ensuring data integrity and curatorial flexibility. Navigation improvements include merging separate On View and Public Collections maps into a single, filterable map and converting the chronology into an interactive timeline. Overall, the project delivers a more intuitive user experience and positions the Foundation's digital presence to support its mission of promoting Rauschenberg's artistic and philanthropic legacyrauschenbergfoundation.org.

submenu.label: Jack Daniels
submenu.projectTitle: Jack Daniels: Building A Global Website with Arnold Worldwide
submenu.project_haiku:
Tennessee tradition flows
Craft distilled through digital care
Heritage meets innovation
submenu.project_footer_CTA: Ready to distill your brand's essence into compelling digital experiences? Let's craft something that honors tradition while embracing the future.
submenu.pageSummary:
Introduction to the Client
Jack Daniel's is one of the world's best‑known whiskey brands. The brand is produced at the Jack Daniel Distillery in Lynchburg, Tennessee and has been owned by the Brown–Forman Corporation since 1956. Jack Daniel's Tennessee whiskey is packaged in distinctive square bottles and sold on a massive scale; its "Black Label" expression alone sold 12.9 million nine‑litre cases in 2017, and the broader family of products—Tennessee Honey, Tennessee Apple, Gentleman Jack, Tennessee Fire and ready‑to‑drink variations—has generated more than 16.1 million equivalent casesen.wikipedia.org. The distillery itself is the oldest registered distillery in the United Statesglobenewswire.com, giving the brand an historic prestige that few spirits can match.

Project Background and Partners
By 2012 Jack Daniel's needed a modern digital experience that honoured its heritage while meeting the expectations of a mobile audience. The company partnered with Arnold Worldwide—an advertising agency founded in 1946 and now part of the Havas Creative Group—to create the new jackdaniels.com. Arnold is a global communications agency that has been one of the most creatively awarded agencies of the past decadeglobenewswire.com, serving clients ranging from Progressive Insurance and Sam's Club to McDonald's and Volvoglobenewswire.com. Knectar was engaged to provide technical consultation, development and back‑end Drupal architecture while Arnold's front‑end team handled the design and user‑interface developmentknectar.com.

A key goal of the project was to create a responsively designed website that adapts to desktops, tablets and mobile devicesglobenewswire.com. The site needed to provide a global experience—serving up localised content to visitors from different countries—while telling the brand's 137‑year story through multimediaglobenewswire.com. In addition to rich storytelling, Jack Daniel's wanted to offer product information, distillery‑visit details, recipes and e‑commerce links in a single, cohesive experienceglobenewswire.com.

Challenges

  • Legal compliance and localisation: As an alcoholic‑beverage brand, Jack Daniel's had to verify a visitor's legal drinking age and comply with differing age requirements across markets. It also had to tailor content (language, privacy notices and available products) based on the visitor's country.
  • Rich storytelling: The client wanted an engaging way to present its long history and unique culture using multimedia while keeping the site manageable for content editors.
  • Product and registration workflows: Beyond brand storytelling, the site needed to provide detailed product information, allow enthusiasts to register special bottles and encourage exploration of cocktail recipes and experiences.
  • Technical integration: The site would run on a Windows Server/IIS/MS SQL stack, and it needed to consume Brown‑Forman's SOAP‑based web services for tasks such as age verification and form submissionsknectar.com. Drupal had to be tailored to this environment while remaining performant and secure.

Solution

Partnership and Agile Delivery
Knectar and Arnold adopted an agile approach that allowed the team to move from concept to launch in only 15 weeksglobenewswire.com. Arnold's designers delivered client‑facing code to a shared repository while Knectar focused on back‑end architecture, integrating Drupal with external web services and ensuring the site's responsive behaviourknectar.com. This collaboration allowed creative and technical teams to iterate quickly without blocking one another.

Age Gate and Country‑specific Content
The site opens with an age‑verification gate. Visitors select their country and language and enter their birth date; a web‑service call (ValidateLDA) checks the legal drinking age for the selected country and denies access if the visitor is underage. The system stores the visitor's country in a session cookie for two hours, enabling Drupal to filter content by country. Localised footers, privacy statements, terms of use and feature content are displayed according to the selected country, and the age gate can toggle features such as cookie tick boxes for jurisdictions like the UK and Ireland.

Multimedia Timeline
To tell the brand's history, the team built a vertical "Our Story" timeline. A feature content type supports a multimedia slideshow at the top, with fields for titles, up to four images or videos, captions and call‑to‑action buttons. Below the feature, the timeline includes stamps and spotlights. Stamps display circular thumbnails on the left and hold fields for images, titles, descriptions and multiple calls to action. Spotlights appear on the right and have fields for number images, titles, descriptions and media galleries. Content editors can control the order of timeline items through weight fields and promote specific items to the top. When visitors access the site, they are greeted by this scrolling multimedia timeline that mixes videos, photos, product information, company news and historical factsglobenewswire.com. Facebook "Like" and Comment widgets integrate social engagement into spotlight details.

Product Gateway and Detail Pages
The product gateway showcases Jack Daniel's four primary product lines—Gentleman Jack, Tennessee Honey, Old No. 7 and Single Barrel—and provides entry points to detailed pages for each. Drupal's content types were used to manage both primary and secondary products. Primary detail pages feature a WYSIWYG‑controlled header for custom imagery and text, a media gallery, related recipes and cross‑links to other products. Secondary products are presented as a list with mouse‑over views and fields for titles, volumes, call‑to‑action links and publish dates.

Register‑Your‑Bottle Workflow
Enthusiasts can register commemorative bottles via a detailed form. Users first select a product and then enter information such as bottle number, personal details (name, address, birth date, email), and contact preferences. The form also includes survey questions about how often visitors drink Jack Daniel's and their likelihood of recommending the brand. Drupal captures the data and passes it to Brown‑Forman's CRM via a web‑service call. This workflow allows the brand to build a global consumer database while respecting regional opt‑in preferences.

Recipes, Experiences and Visit Us
Separate content types manage recipes and experiences. Recipe nodes include fields for titles, images, ingredient lists and instructions, while experience nodes have titles, images, descriptions and call‑to‑action links. Both content types support country tags so that only relevant items appear based on the visitor's age‑gate selection. The "Visit Us" page and the privacy and registration pages are managed through WYSIWYG fields, enabling editors to update text and imagery without developer intervention.

Technical Details
The project used Drupal 7 as the CMS and was deployed on a Windows Server 2008 R2/IIS 7.5 environment with an MS SQL 2005 database and PHP 5.3 via FastCGI. Although Drupal is more commonly hosted on Linux/Apache stacks, the team replicated the production environment in development to surface and resolve compatibility issues. Advanced SOAP web‑service connectors were developed to integrate with Brown‑Forman's systems for age verification, country lists and registration dataknectar.com. The responsive front‑end was built using HTML5 and CSS3 so that the same codebase adapts gracefully to desktops, tablets and mobile devicesglobenewswire.com.

Results and Impact

  • Global reach: The new jackdaniels.com launched in June 2012 as the brand's first responsive site and quickly rolled out to 185 countries with seven English‑language versions and plans for localisationglobenewswire.com. Country‑specific cookies and content tagging allowed the brand to tailor the experience to local regulations and preferences without duplicating the entire site.
  • Rich brand storytelling: The immersive timeline, product galleries and recipe/experience sections gave visitors an insider's look at Jack Daniel's history and culture. The combination of multimedia storytelling and social‑media integration encouraged deeper engagementglobenewswire.com.
  • Compliance and data capture: The age gate and bottle‑registration workflow ensured legal compliance and enabled Jack Daniel's to collect opt‑in consumer data across markets. Server‑side validation and web‑service integration reduced errors and manual work.
  • Agile delivery and maintainability: Thanks to the agile partnership between Arnold and Knectar, the project was completed from concept to launch in only 15 weeksglobenewswire.com. The use of Drupal content types and WYSIWYG fields empowers content editors to manage and update the site without ongoing developer involvement.

Conclusion
Jack Daniel's global website exemplifies how thoughtful collaboration between creative and technical teams can translate a storied heritage into a modern digital experience. By combining Arnold Worldwide's brand storytelling and design expertise with Knectar's enterprise Drupal development, the project delivered a responsive, legally compliant and globally localised platform that honours Jack Daniel's past while serving the needs of today's connected consumers. The case demonstrates that an agile approach, backed by flexible CMS architecture and strong partner collaboration, can bring complex websites to market quickly without sacrificing quality or regulatory compliance.

Appendix: Site Feature Summary
The key functional areas of the site are summarised below. Each item lists its purpose and highlights the Drupal implementation that supported it:

  • Age Gate – verifies a visitor's legal drinking age and stores their country selection. A call to the ValidateLDA web service compares the entered birth date against the legal age for the selected country and, if approved, Drupal stores the country in a session cookie. This cookie drives localisation of footers, terms and other content.
  • Timeline – presents the brand's history through a vertical timeline of multimedia content. The timeline uses three Drupal content types: a feature type for a slideshow at the top, stamps that appear on the left with images and descriptions, and spotlights that appear on the right with number images, descriptions and media galleries.
  • Product Gateway – showcases Jack Daniel's product lines and links to detail pages. Primary and secondary product content types manage custom headers, media galleries and cross‑links to related products.
  • Bottle Registration – collects data from consumers who register commemorative bottles. The Drupal form includes fields for bottle number, personal information and preferences, then posts the data to Brown‑Forman's CRM via a web‑service call.
  • Recipes & Experiences – inspire enthusiasts with cocktail recipes and brand experiences. Separate content types hold titles, images, ingredient lists and instructions; country tags ensure that only relevant items appear.
  • Visit Us & Privacy – provide distillery information and legal notices. These pages use WYSIWYG fields so content managers can update text and images easily, and multiple versions can be created for different countries.

submenu.label: Studio Arts Consortium International (SACI), Florence
submenu.project_haiku:
Renaissance returns
Art blooms in Florence once more
Creativity crosses oceans
submenu.project_footer_CTA: Ready to help students discover their artistic passion abroad? Let's create digital experiences that inspire global creativity and cultural exchange.
submenu.pageSummary:
Client background
Studio Arts College International (SACI) is a U.S.‑accredited art school in Florence, Italy. It was founded in 1975 by Fulbright scholar and painter Jules Maidoff and is the oldest American art school in Florence. SACI holds the distinction of being the first art school in Europe accredited by the National Association of Schools of Art and Design (NASAD). Over several decades SACI has welcomed thousands of students pursuing degrees or study abroad experiences in studio art, design, conservation and art history. Students study in two historical palazzi—Palazzo dei Cartelloni and Palazzo Maidoff—located in Florence's historic center Palazzo dei Cartelloni is a 17th‑century Renaissance palace built for mathematician Vincenzo Viviani, a pupil of Galileo Galilei; its façade describes Galileo's discoveries and the interior features painted ceilings and frescoed walls. Palazzo Maidoff is two blocks from the Duomo and offers studio spaces around a courtyard. Studying in these landmark buildings underscores SACI's prestige and connection to the Renaissance tradition.

Project overview
Objective. SACI's communications team and Stoltze Design partnered to redesign SACI's website and digital identity. The goal was to simplify and streamline SACI's extensive information, modernize its visual identity, and create a responsive, user‑friendly site that showcases programs, admissions, student life, events and galleries. The redesign was part of a broader rebranding effort; Stoltze introduced a new logo that blended traditional proportions with bold color and graceful typography to reflect SACI's commitment to excellence and accessibility.

Initial state & challenges. Prior to redesign, SACI maintained a complex platform containing years of content. Stakeholders reported that information architecture, navigation, and page layouts made it difficult for prospective students to discover programs or apply. Christina Gednalske, who led ongoing content management, explains that the Drupal redesign involved large‑scale content migration and responsive design, creating robust directories, forms, unique page templates and an extensive sitemap covering students, admissions, courses, events, galleries, faculty, blog pieces and alumni. Even after launch, continual additions and updates were needed to address feedback from board members, faculty, staff, prospective and admitted students, and alumni. The communications team sought to maintain user friendliness while adapting to these changes.

Scope. Working remotely from Florence with Stoltze Design in Boston, the team established goals for the redesign: simplify and streamline the vast content, update the UI, create a responsive experience across desktop, mobile and tablet, make learning about programs easy and enticing, and improve and simplify the application and admissions process. Additionally, the site needed to capture the atmosphere of Florence while conveying credibility comparable to top U.S. art and design schools.

Design solution and implementation

Extensive sitemap & user flows: The team designed a comprehensive sitemap based on typical user journeys for prospective and admitted students, parents, study‑abroad advisors, alumni, faculty and board members. Iterative sitemapping and user flows considered research and application steps, academic information needs, student life queries and alumni engagement. Drupal's flexible taxonomy system was used to organize content by degree type, term, course category, faculty type and other vocabularies.

Content types & templates: The project created tailored content types such as Programs, Courses, Classes, Faculty/Alumni, Events & Exhibitions, Blog (News) and Student Gallery. Each content type included custom fields (e.g., term, degree type, category) and standardized templates for list and detail views. For example, Program pages display degree type headers, descriptions and a grid of programs driven by taxonomy. Course pages include filters by term and category and dynamically list classes. Events lists use date fields to show upcoming events and an event carousel on the home page.

User roles & permissions: The site defined roles for administrators, editors and faculty, with Drupal's revision and publishing controls enabled by default. This allowed controlled content updates while ensuring that only published content is visible to visitors.

Visual design & user experience
New identity: Stoltze Design created a new logo and brand system that merges traditional proportion with contemporary typography and bold color, mirroring SACI's blend of Renaissance tradition and modern accessibility.

Full‑page scroll & responsive layout: The home page uses a full‑page scroll to present sections such as hero media, promoted programs, news grid and event carousel. A custom script transforms the header into a fixed "mini‑header" on scroll. Responsive design ensures that the site functions seamlessly on desktops, tablets and mobile devices.

Hero media & storytelling: Administrators can choose a hero image or embedded video (YouTube or Vimeo) for the home page; the video field overrides the image when present. WYSIWYG fields allow for customizable taglines such as "College of Art…" and "Florence, Italy". These elements give visitors an immediate sense of SACI's location and mission.

Promoted items & dynamic carousels: A promoted items field collection lets administrators spotlight programs with an image, category, title, description and call‑to‑action button. The home page also contains a news grid showing the five most recent blog posts and an event carousel that displays upcoming events marked "promoted to home page". Pagination and text blocks provide additional context and link to full articles or events.

Navigation & global elements: The site features a top navigation linking to Alumni, Request Information and Apply pages; a main navigation listing primary sections like About and Academics; and a footer with links back to the home page, contact blocks, social media links and WYSIWYG areas for facility hours and contact information. Drupal's search module provides site‑wide search.

Accessibility & usability: Custom block placements allow administrators to insert calls‑to‑action (e.g., "Take the next steps…" banner) within specific regions. The site integrates Chosen for enhanced select boxes, Google Analytics for tracking, Metatag for SEO, and ShareThis for social sharing. The domain is configured to redirect all variants, ensuring consistency and security.

Technology stack
CMS: The entire site runs on Drupal, selected for its flexible content model, taxonomy system and robust module ecosystem. Custom content types, fields and views were built to accommodate SACI's complex information architecture.

Front‑end: Responsive layouts were built using HTML5/CSS and JavaScript. The full‑page scroll effect and header transformation rely on custom JS. The design follows the brand guidelines established by Stoltze, ensuring consistency across devices.

Third‑party services: Video hosting uses YouTube and Vimeo. Social sharing is handled via ShareThis, and analytics through Google Analytics. SEO metadata is controlled via the Metatag module.

Impact and results
After launch, SACI and Stoltze reported measurable improvements:

Enhanced accessibility and user experience. Stoltze notes that the redesigned website improved accessibility for applicants and administrative staff and provided a streamlined application process. Flexible content components made it easier for staff to update pages and showcase student stories and events.

Increased engagement and enrollment. SACI reported a boost in enrollment following the site's launch. The new design and improved application workflows likely contributed to higher conversion rates.

Ongoing adaptability. Continuous updates to information architecture, UX writing, content and page layouts have maintained the site's relevance as SACI's programs evolve. The flexible Drupal framework and modular design support these iterations without major overhauls.

Conclusion
The collaboration between Studio Arts College International, Stoltze Design and the Knectar development team yielded a comprehensive redesign of SACI's digital presence. Grounded in the institution's rich history and prestige, the project delivered a modern, responsive website that simplifies complex information, enhances the user journey and reflects SACI's blend of Renaissance heritage and contemporary art education. By leveraging Drupal's flexible CMS, thoughtful information architecture, dynamic storytelling components and a refreshed visual identity, the new site not only improved internal workflows but also increased prospective student engagement and enrollment. The project demonstrates how strategic design and content management can revitalize an educational institution's online identity while honoring its historical roots.

submenu.pageSummary:
Client Background
The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, established in 1903, stands as one of Boston's most prestigious cultural institutions and a jewel of American art museums. Founded by the visionary collector Isabella Stewart Gardner, the museum houses an extraordinary collection of European, Asian, and American art in an intimate Venetian-style palace setting. With world-renowned masterpieces by artists including Rembrandt, Vermeer, Sargent, and Whistler, the Gardner maintains its founder's vision of displaying art in a personal, unconventional manner that continues to inspire visitors from around the globe.

Challenge
The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum needed to modernize their digital presence while maintaining the intimate, personal character that defines the institution. The primary challenges included:

  • Complex Content Architecture: Managing diverse content types including historic art collections, events, exhibitions, stories, audio content, and room details
  • Collections Integration: Seamlessly integrating data from Embark Collections management system with over 2,500 art objects
  • Multi-faceted User Experience: Serving diverse audiences from art enthusiasts to researchers to casual visitors
  • Interactive Features: Creating engaging digital experiences that reflect the museum's unique storytelling approach
  • Content Management: Empowering museum staff with flexible, user-friendly content management capabilities

Solution
Technical Architecture
We implemented a robust Drupal 8 solution with sophisticated third-party integrations:

Core CMS Framework:

  • Drupal 8 with custom content types and taxonomies
  • Advanced user role management (Root/Admin, Editor, Author, Contributor)
  • Flexible paragraph-based content architecture for dynamic page building

Collections Integration:

  • Embark Collections System: Real-time XML data integration for art object metadata
  • eMuseum Integration: Enhanced digital asset management and display capabilities
  • Automated vocabulary management for artists, centuries, countries, and object categories

Advanced Features:

  • Interactive audio player with LibSyn integration
  • Advanced filtering and search capabilities across all content types
  • Dynamic room mapping and wayfinding
  • Multi-media story chapters with before/after sliders, video, and audio components

Content Strategy & User Experience
Working closely with Fabrique's design team, we developed a content strategy that honored the museum's unique character:

Immersive Storytelling:

  • Custom "Story" content type supporting up to 15 interactive chapters
  • Multiple chapter formats: intro slides, text/image combinations, quotes, videos, before/after comparisons, mini-slideshows, and gallery sliders
  • Integrated audio commentary with curator insights

Collections Discovery:

  • Sophisticated filtering system by artist, room, century, country, and object type
  • Featured art carousels with high-resolution imagery
  • Related content algorithms connecting artworks by artist, period, and location

Event & Exhibition Management:

  • Dynamic calendar with advanced filtering by artist, event type, and tags
  • Promotional panel system for featured exhibitions
  • Integrated ticketing and visitor information

Room Experience:

  • Interactive room detail pages with conservation insights
  • Floor-based navigation and filtering
  • "Rooms Nearby" recommendations for enhanced wayfinding

Technical Innovations

Custom Taxonomies & Data Management:

  • 12 specialized vocabularies managing everything from audio genres to room locations
  • Automated mapping between internal room codes and visitor-friendly room names
  • Smart content relationships driving "related content" recommendations

Media Integration:

  • Vimeo integration for video content
  • Custom audio player with playlist capabilities
  • High-resolution image display with zoom functionality and Creative Commons licensing

User-Centric Features:

  • Accessibility compliance with high-contrast mode
  • Mobile-responsive design optimized for on-site visitor use
  • Emergency banner system for real-time visitor communications
  • Google Places API integration for accurate hours and closure notifications

Results & Impact
The new digital platform successfully transformed the Gardner Museum's online presence:

Enhanced User Experience:

  • Intuitive navigation reflecting the museum's physical layout
  • Rich multimedia content bringing collections to life digitally
  • Seamless integration between planning visits and exploring collections

Operational Efficiency:

  • Streamlined content management with role-based permissions
  • Automated data synchronization reducing manual content updates
  • Flexible page-building tools empowering staff to create engaging content

Technical Excellence:

  • Scalable architecture supporting future growth and integrations
  • Robust search and filtering capabilities handling complex collection metadata
  • Performance-optimized delivery of high-resolution images and multimedia content
