Code becomes canvas
Pixels dance to algorithm
Art born from logic
submenu.project_footer_CTA: Ready to bring your creative vision to life through code? Let's make art together.
submenu.pageSummary:
Generative Sketches by Knectar

Introduction
The four sketches shared by Knectar are examples of generative art built with the p5.js library. Each sketch uses algorithmic rules to create evolving visual patterns. Understanding these sketches requires looking at the underlying code and the mathematical ideas that drive them. Concepts like vector arithmetic, Bézier curves, Perlin noise (a smooth pseudo‑random function used for organic motion), linear interpolation and perspective geometry are used to produce the graphics. This case‑study summarises how each sketch works and highlights the key technical ideas.

Perspective Trace

Overview. The perspective trace sketch depicts hundreds of translucent rectangles radiating from a moving vanishing point. The rectangles feel like panes of coloured glass receding to a point in space. The algorithm:

  • Initialize parameters. Variables set the line thickness, the number of rectangles, a vanishing point (vanPoint) and arrays to track individual rectangles and the vanishing point's trail. Colour mode is set to HSB for smooth hue transitions and angleMode(DEGREES) simplifies angle computations.
  • Create rectangles. The Recto class holds two static edges (edgeT and edgeB), randomly placed on the canvas, and calculates dynamic vertices that converge at the vanishing point. On each frame, the method updateEdgePos() computes the intersection of the lines from the vanishing point to the static edges.
  • Draw rectangles. In drawReact() the rectangle is drawn as a quadrilateral using the static edge endpoints and the dynamically calculated vanishing‑point vertices. Semi‑transparent fills with varying hues are used for depth and layering.
  • Animate vanishing point. A updateVanPoint() function moves the vanishing point along a path defined by sinusoidal functions:

vanPoint.x = vanPoint.x + cos(frameCount/2 + vanPoint.y/2);
vanPoint.y = vanPoint.y - sin(frameCount - vanPoint.x/2);
ellipse(vanPoint.x, vanPoint.y, 5);
vanPointArray.push(createVector(vanPoint.x, vanPoint.y));

Key concept – perspective projection. By treating each rectangle's top and bottom edges as two lines receding toward the vanishing point, the sketch mimics linear perspective. Changing the vanishing point's position causes all rectangles to re‑compute their dynamic vertices, resulting in a shifting illusion of depth.

Tess_animation (Dynamic Tessellation)

Overview. This sketch animates curves that connect moving anchor points along the edges of a square. Each side of the square has dotCount anchors and every frame the anchor positions oscillate along their respective edges. Curves (Bézier segments) connect pairs of anchors according to a shuffled sequence, giving a perpetual re‑weaving of lines.

Algorithm.

  • Setup. squareSize is set to half of the canvas height, defining the size of the square. A totalDots value equal to four times dotCount calculates how many anchors reside along the square's perimeter. A random order array (randArray) is generated and shuffled; it determines the order in which anchors will be connected.
  • Anchor placement. In the Anchor class, the function initAnchorArray() divides each side into equal segments. For each of the dotCount positions, it creates four anchor points: one on the top ("T"), one on the right ("R"), one on the bottom ("B") and one on the left ("L").
  • Anchor motion. In every frame, cycleAnchors() moves each anchor along its side. For top or bottom anchors the x‑coordinate is updated by adding a cosine term cos(frameCount/pace[i]*3), and for left or right anchors the y‑coordinate changes similarly.
  • Connecting anchors. The connectAnchors() method uses pairs of indices from randArray to decide which anchors to link. Conditional blocks determine how to call the bezier() function so that each connection curves inward and respects the geometry of the square.

Key concept – oscillating anchors and Bézier curves. The motion of anchors uses sinusoidal functions to create smooth back‑and‑forth movement. Randomizing the connection order means that the network of curves continuously reconfigures.

Blobby (Smooth Noise‑Driven Blob)

Overview. The Blobby test sketch generates an organic, irregular blob that drifts across the screen. The blob's shape is determined by sampling Perlin noise over polar coordinates. Perlin noise produces smooth random values, which are used here to modulate the radius of each point on a circle.

Algorithm.

  • Parameters. A centre point center is defined; r0 sets the base radius, dr defines how much the radius can fluctuate and rn scales the input to the noise function. A time variable t advances slowly to animate the noise field.
  • Drawing the blob. In draw() the code begins a new shape (beginShape()) and loops through angles theta from 0 to 2π, incrementing by one degree. For each angle it computes a noise‑modulated radius r using:

r = r0 + map(noise(rn + rn * cos(theta), rn + rn * sin(theta), t),
            0, 1, -dr, dr);

The p5.js noise() function returns a smooth value between 0 and 1. The two‑argument call (cos(theta) and sin(theta)) means that nearby angles sample nearby points in the noise field.

  • Motion. After drawing, center.x is incremented by a small value (0.5), causing the blob to drift horizontally. The time variable t increments as well, making the noise field evolve.

Key concept – Perlin noise on a circle. By sampling noise with coordinates (rn + rn*cos(theta), rn + rn*sin(theta), t) the algorithm effectively traverses a circular slice of the 3D noise field. This ensures that the radius at angle θ is similar to that at neighbouring angles but different around the full circle.

Zag Connector (Noise Pen)

Overview. The final sketch draws scribbly lines that connect a sequence of grid cells. It uses a class Zag to choose random cells and draw lines between them using Perlin noise to vary the stroke weight (thickness). The visual result is a set of organic, hand‑drawn paths that appear to meander through the grid.

Algorithm.

  • Grid creation. The canvas is divided into a grid of cells (cellSize = 111 pixels). Each Cell stores its position and has methods to draw its outline or highlight itself.
  • Generating a path. When a new Zag is created, it randomly selects between four and six cells. The method setArr() picks random cells from gridArr and stores their positions in an array; it also pushes the first point again to close the loop.
  • Drawing segments. The animateLineNoise(index) function draws a more scribbly line. It loops a parameter i from 0 to 100 and linearly interpolates positions between curr and next but then changes the stroke weight using Perlin noise:

tempX = map(i, 0, 100, curr.x, next.x, 1);
tempY = map(i, 0, 100, curr.y, next.y, 1);
thickness = noise(xOff, yOff) * 33;
strokeWeight(thickness);
point(tempX, tempY);
xOff += 0.006;

Because noise() returns a smooth value between 0 and 1, the stroke thickness varies gradually along the segment. The point() function draws individual dots that collectively form a jittery line.

Key concept – noise‑modulated drawing. Perlin noise is used here to vary stroke thickness along a line. The result is similar to drawing with a pen whose pressure changes continuously; the lines feel alive and organic.

Summary

The four sketches illustrate how relatively simple algorithms can produce compelling generative artwork. In the perspective trace, a moving vanishing point creates continuously shifting perspectives by recalculating the intersection of rectangles with the vanishing‑point lines. Tess_animation uses oscillating anchor points and shuffled Bézier connections to weave dynamic patterns within a square. Blobby samples Perlin noise around a circle to form an irregular, evolving blob. Zag connector combines grid navigation and noise‑modulated drawing to create hand‑drawn paths.

Common threads across these sketches include using trigonometric functions for periodic motion, using noise() for organic variation and mapping arrays of points to generate geometry. Together, they demonstrate the expressive potential of algorithmic drawing in p5.js.

From p5.js Bézier‑curve Sketch to AxiDraw Pen Plotter

This case study explains how a generative p5.js sketch that builds a set of Bézier curves can be exported to a pen plotter workflow. It looks at the algorithm used to generate the curves, how to export the design as a vector file, modify it in Inkscape, convert it to G‑code and visualise it, and finally draw it with an AxiDraw v3 pen plotter.

1. Creating a Bézier‑curve design in p5.js

1.1 Algorithmic construction of the curves
The provided sketch builds two closed shapes (shape1 and shape2) defined by arrays of anchor points and control vectors. In setup, the code chooses random grid intersections for each anchor and snaps coordinates to the grid spacing using a helper function snapToGrid. The function randomSnappedControlPoint picks a random angle and distance around each anchor, creates a temporary control vector and snaps it to the grid, ensuring that the Bézier handles align to the same grid. Each shape thus has n anchors with associated control vectors. The sketch later draws cubic Bézier segments between consecutive anchors; symmetric control points generate smooth transitions.

The draw loop performs interpolation between the two shapes. It computes an interpolated shape by linearly mixing the anchor positions and control vectors of shape1 and shape2 by a slider value t (0‒1). For each interpolated shape, the sketch optionally computes a colour gradient by interpolating between two user‑selectable colours using lerpColor. It then draws a closed loop of Bézier curves with drawClosedLoop(). A toggle button controls whether the intermediate shapes display control points; another slider controls the number of transitional shapes to be drawn, producing layered gradient lines. Because all anchors and control points are snapped to the grid, the resulting curves maintain consistent spacing and a structured appearance.

1.2 Exporting as SVG from p5.js
To move the design into a vector‑graphics workflow, the sketch uses the p5.plotSvg library. This library is designed specifically for exporting SVG files tailored for path‑based output devices such as the AxiDraw pen‑plotter. The library writes SVG files that describe only the geometry of paths rather than their visual style, reflecting the fact that plotting machines interpret line paths physically. Because p5.plotSvg does not interfere with p5.js's normal graphics output and is easy to add to projects, it provides an unobtrusive way to record the drawn shapes. When the sketch's "SVG export" button is pressed, it creates a temporary SVG graphics buffer, replays the drawing commands into that buffer and uses save() to download the resulting SVG.

2. Editing the vector design in Inkscape

After exporting the design, the next step is to refine it in a vector‑editing program. Inkscape is a free, open‑source vector graphics editor whose workflow is based on vector objects. It includes tools for creating rectangles, ellipses, stars, polygons and spirals, and these objects can be filled with solid colours, patterns or gradients. Inkscape also provides Bézier and calligraphic tools for drawing curves and allows transformations such as moving, rotating, scaling and skewing. The Edit Path by Node tool supports editing individual nodes and handles of Bézier paths. These features make it straightforward to open the exported SVG, adjust control points or proportions, combine or remove paths, and add annotations or layout marks. Inkscape's primary file format is SVG, and it can export to many other vector and image formats, making it a good intermediate step before generating machine code.

3. Converting SVG to G‑code

3.1 Using Universal G‑code Sender (UGS)
To drive a CNC machine or pen plotter, the vector drawing must be converted into G‑code. The Universal G‑code Sender (UGS) is a free, cross‑platform application for interfacing with CNC controllers such as GRBL, FluidNC and TinyG. UGS runs on Windows, macOS, Linux and Raspberry Pi and includes a configurable user interface with a 3D G‑code visualiser that colour‑codes segments and shows real‑time tool‑position feedback. It supports real‑time overrides, a built‑in G‑code editor and a designer editor that can optimise G‑code (removing comments, truncating decimal precision and converting arcs to line segments). Users can load the edited SVG or DXF into a plugin or a separate CAM tool to convert the paths into G‑code, then open the resulting file in UGS.

3.2 Previewing with NC Viewer
Before plotting, it is good practice to verify the G‑code. NC Viewer is a web‑based G‑code simulator and viewer. According to an overview of G‑code simulators, NC Viewer offers a simple yet powerful interface for visualising G‑code programs and simulating tool movements. It provides real‑time rendering of the toolpath, allowing users to analyse the machining process dynamically and includes features like zooming, panning and layer highlighting for better analysis and understanding of the G‑code data. By loading the G‑code into NC Viewer, the designer can confirm that the sequence of moves matches the intended drawing and that there are no unexpected rapid moves or tool plunges.

4. Plotting with AxiDraw V3

The final stage is to physically draw the design with an AxiDraw pen‑plotter. The AxiDraw V3/A3 is a larger version of the AxiDraw V3 and is designed to write or draw on 11×17‑inch (A3) paper. It is described by its manufacturer as "the original simple, modern, precise and versatile pen plotter," capable of writing or drawing on almost any flat surface. The machine can hold fountain pens, permanent markers and other implements and has a writing head that extends beyond its base so it can draw on objects larger than the machine itself. AxiDraw plotters support a variety of applications; the V3/A3 model includes custom‑made aluminium extrusions and precision‑machined components for improved precision and robustness. Using the AxiDraw's companion software, the user loads the G‑code generated earlier, chooses a pen, secures the paper and runs the plot.

4.1 Why pen plotters?
Plotting the generative design with a pen plotter allows the smooth Bézier curves to be realised as continuous ink lines rather than rasterised pixels. Because the p5.js sketch snapped control points to a grid, the resulting curves have a mechanical quality that translates well to plotting. The gradient‑based layering can be reproduced by swapping pens or by drawing multiple passes with different inks.

5. Summary of the end‑to‑end workflow

  • Generate the artwork. In p5.js, random grid intersections produce anchor points, control points are placed on the grid and smoothed by snapping functions, and the sketch interpolates between shapes with colour gradients. The design is recorded as an SVG using p5.plotSvg, which exports the geometry of the paths.
  • Refine in Inkscape. Open the SVG in Inkscape, use node and path tools to fine‑tune curves, combine or split paths and adjust layout. Inkscape supports a wide variety of vector shapes and transformations and allows direct editing of Bézier nodes.
  • Generate G‑code. Use a CAM extension or plugin to convert the edited SVG into G‑code. Load the file into Universal G‑code Sender, which includes a 3D visualiser, real‑time overrides and G‑code editing options.
  • Verify toolpaths. Preview the G‑code in NC Viewer to ensure the toolpaths follow the desired pattern and that there are no collisions or unwanted motions. NC Viewer provides real‑time toolpath rendering and interactive controls for analysis.
  • Draw on AxiDraw. Secure paper on the AxiDraw v3, load the verified G‑code, choose pens and run the plotter. The pen plotter's ability to draw on almost any flat surface and its extended writing head make it suitable for large or unconventional media.

Conclusion

This pipeline demonstrates how generative code can be transformed into tangible artwork through careful consideration of algorithms, file formats and hardware capabilities. Each tool plays a specific role: p5.js enables procedural composition; p5.plotSvg records vector geometry; Inkscape refines and prepares the artwork; UGS converts and previews machine instructions; NC Viewer verifies toolpaths; and the AxiDraw physically renders the design.

Materials, Processes and the Spirit of Experiments in Material and Flow

Introduction
Chris Amato's first solo exhibition, Experiments in Material and Flow, brings together fifteen to twenty small‐scale sculptures that merge the artist's passions for algorithmic design, structural geology and fluid dynamics. The artist statement notes that the work explores "material contrast, experimentation in fabrication and fastening techniques, and tension." Each piece is an "invention" that balances naturalistic forces—deformation, fluid flow, and chemical or mechanical processes—against the human hand and eye. Objects range from the size of a baseball to that of a small dog and are wall‑mounted to encourage close engagement. The following discussion explores the media and processes employed, revealing how the materials and methods serve the overall narrative.

1. Stone and Plaster Forms

Pieces are carved or cast from dense materials such as stone, plaster or concrete. One polished, ovoid form has the smooth tactility of a river‑worn pebble; its subtle gradients of grey and the soft transition between planes evoke the erosion and abrasion of natural processes. Another piece resembles a fluid mass carved from stone, with deep undercuts and tapered limbs; its matte surface and gentle undulations highlight the artist's careful hand sanding. A stacked tower of rough, slab‑like elements recalls geological strata; the alternating courses suggest sedimentary layering, while a blue accent hints at a vein of mineral. These works draw directly on the artist's background in structural geology, translating processes of weathering, deposition and deformation into intimate objects.

Process: The polished finish and consistent textures suggest a combination of CNC carving and hand finishing. Some forms are cast in plaster or concrete using silicone molds and then sanded smooth. Others, like the stacked tower, could be assembled from individual cast blocks that are hand‑stacked or joined. The balance between machine precision and hand touch echoes the show's theme of tension between natural forces and human intervention.

2. Wire and Tension Constructions

A second group consists of delicate, linear constructions made from wire or slender rods. One work forms a star‑like constellation of thin sticks connected at varying angles; some elements are painted red, introducing a visual tension. Another piece resembles a spherical gyroscope or atom model: concentric spirals of wire encircle an orange, vessel‑like core. A more open construction arcs gracefully from a central point, with slender wires describing loops and curves in space. These works explore balance, gravity and tension. They capture the moment when forces are in equilibrium yet seem perpetually on the verge of collapse, mirroring natural phenomena like plant tendrils or fluid flow.

Process: The sculptures are hand‑constructed by cutting, bending and joining steel or brass rods. Fastening techniques could include soldering or mechanical fixes such as sleeves or clamps. The subtle asymmetries and slight imperfections emphasize their handmade quality. Some pieces incorporate suspended elements (as in the orange "pendulum"), introducing movement and changing the viewer's perception as they navigate around the work.

3. Wood and CNC‑Carved Forms

The exhibition also includes several fluid, organic forms carved from wood. A pair of sinuous, interlocking shapes carved from warm hardwood evokes the cresting of waves or the growth of shells. The continuity of grain across the curves hints that they were carved from a single block. Another piece combines wood and a white synthetic material: wooden arms emerge from a central white volume, creating a dynamic interplay between natural and engineered surfaces. These sculptures highlight the material's warmth and directional grain while exploring twisting and folding motions inspired by fluid dynamics.

Process: The crisp edges and smooth surfaces employ the use of CNC milling to rough out the forms, followed by extensive hand sanding to refine transitions and achieve an inviting tactile quality. The combination of materials may involve laminating wood and resin, then carving them together. The joinery between dissimilar materials is seamless, reflecting careful planning and an understanding of mechanical fastening and adhesives.

4. Cast Metal Pieces

Some work is cast in metal. A silvery, wing‑like form sits atop a plinth; its pitted surface and irregular edges evoke a geological outcrop or a piece of driftwood. Another image shows an open, boat‑shaped volume made from a folded sheet of metal, suggesting both vessel and wing. These works introduce a metallic sheen that contrasts with the matte surfaces of stone and wood, adding to the exhibition's material diversity.

Process: The wing‑like piece could be sand‑cast in aluminium or another non‑ferrous alloy, where the artist sculpts a wax or foam positive, creates a mould, pours molten metal and then cleans and polishes the cast. The folded sheet may be fabricated by cutting and bending sheet metal, then welding or brazing seams. These processes underscore the artist's interest in transforming industrial materials through handcrafted intervention.

5. Resin, 3D‑Printed and Mixed‑Media Works

Some sculptures combine synthetic materials and digital processes. One piece shows multipled wood, PVC tubes and serpentine forms that are cast in resin; the seamless curves and uniform color. Another piece encloses a white, organic shape within a carved wooden cube, with coloured spheres embedded in the interior. This juxtaposition of materials invites viewers to peer into a microcosm of fluid dynamics. Two related works depict translucent white surfaces edged with deep blue; the forms ripple like fabric caught in motion. The crisp, coloured edges and thin‑walled construction suggest a layered casting or 3D‑printing process followed by hand finishing.

Process: These works likely begin as digital models informed by fluid simulation or algorithmic design. The models are fabricated via additive manufacturing (such as resin stereolithography) or casting in translucent polymer. After printing or casting, the artist sands, polishes and paints edges to emphasise contours. When combined with wood or other materials, the elements are carefully integrated, reflecting the artist's attention to fastening and assembly.

Conclusion

Across media, Chris Amato's Experiments in Material and Flow reveals a deep engagement with geometry, deformation and materiality. Stone and plaster pieces recall geological processes; wire constructions explore tension and balance; wood carvings capture fluid motion; cast metals bring a contrasting sheen; and mixed‑media works introduce digital and synthetic elements. These varied techniques allow the artist to probe the boundary between natural forces and human intervention. The exhibition invites viewers to contemplate how different materials respond to processes of carving, casting, assembling and digitally fabricating, and to feel the underlying currents of balance, tension and sensuality that run through the artist's practice.

From Concept to Pilot Success — The Making of Thing Y

Introduction
Innovative toy Thing Y began as a concept in the mind of web‑designer‑turned‑inventor Chris Amato. Inspired by the idea of bridging imagination and reality, Amato wanted to create a pocket‑sized object that balanced function and beauty. The toy would invite users to explore geometry through tactile play while demonstrating how modern digital tools and fabrication services can accelerate product development. In 2021 Amato introduced Thing Y in Northampton, Massachusetts and the toy quickly sold out during a pilot program at A2Z Science & Learning Store.

Ideation and Early Sketches

Creator background: According to an interview on Inventors Helping Inventors, Chris Amato left a geology career and founded a web‑development agency before designing an innovative toy. His experiences in art, web design and fabrication provided the skills needed to move from concept to production.

Initial sketches: The design process started with hand‑drawn sketches exploring forms that could be built from modular beams connected by magnets. Sketching allowed Amato to quickly iterate on proportions and understand how pieces might join.

Vector drawings with Inkscape: After sketching, Amato digitized the shapes using Inkscape. Inkscape is a free, open‑source vector graphics editor with flexible drawing tools, broad file‑format compatibility and Bezier curves. Vector artwork created in Inkscape could be exported as DXF/SVG files for laser cutting and packaging prototypes.

Digital Modeling and Parametric Design

Rhino 3D modeling: To accurately model the toy's geometry, Amato used Rhino 3D. Rhino is described by its developer as "the most versatile of all 3D modelers," used in many industries. The software excels at translating digital forms into buildable objects, and its parametric tools (via Grasshopper) allowed Amato to test proportions and magnet spacing quickly.

Iterative design: With parametric modeling, changes to beam length, thickness or joint angles could be updated instantly. This iterative workflow enabled rapid exploration of countless configurations before committing to prototypes.

Securing Intellectual Property

To protect the idea, Amato filed a provisional patent. "Patent pending" status means the inventor has submitted a provisional application to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. It gives notice to competitors that a patent is being pursued and establishes priority. The status can be used on packaging and marketing materials while the patent is examined. Filing early allowed Amato to disclose the product publicly during market testing while preserving the right to seek full patent protection later.

Prototyping Phases

Wooden & ruler prototypes: Early models were built using wooden rulers and thin hardwood strips. Magnets were epoxied into the ends to test hinge motion and determine the number of magnets needed for stability. Proved that simple materials could approximate the motion and geometry of the final toy; helped refine magnet strength and spacing.

3D‑printed versions: FDM and resin printers produced beams with integrated slots for magnets. 3D printing allowed exploration of different lengths and cross‑sections without investing in tooling. Provided tactile feedback on ergonomics and magnet fit; highlighted tolerances required for smooth rotation and snapping action.

Laser‑cut prototypes: Once the geometry was finalized, Amato uploaded vector files to Ponoko, an online laser‑cutting service. Ponoko's platform lets customers upload designs, select materials (over 200 laser‑safe options), get automated feedback and receive precise parts quickly. The service produces parts from small one‑off orders to thousands of pieces and delivers them within a day for local orders.

Packaging prototypes with Cricut: To design packaging for retail, Amato used a Cricut Maker. The Cricut is a desktop cutting machine that can draw, score and cut paper or cardstock. Similarly, Amato designed box templates in Inkscape, imported them into Cricut Design Space and cut out small runs of packaging. Allowed low‑cost, custom packaging with precise scoring and decoration; enabled quick iteration of box sizes and insert designs without ordering large quantities.

Pilot Production and Market Testing

A2Z Science & Learning Toy Store
Amato partnered with A2Z Science & Learning Store in Northampton, MA to test market reception. The store listed several variations of Thing Y:

• Crystal‑clear medium set: This set included eight long and two mini beams made from translucent clear acrylic. The product description notes that the magnetic fidget beams "can be configured in nearly infinite ways" and are "satisfying to hold, snap and manipulate". Each long beam measured about 4½ inches long by ½ inch wide, while the mini beams were 2 inches long. The set sold for $19.99 but was marked "out of stock" during the pilot.

• Sassy red big set: This version contained four long and two mini beams cut from translucent red acrylic. The store described the beams similarly as magnetic fidget pieces with "nearly infinite" configurations. It also listed identical dimensions and an out‑of‑stock status, confirming the pilot program sold through its initial inventory.

Discussion: Balancing Digital Precision with Physical Play

Thing Y showcases how modern design and fabrication tools can compress the distance between imagination and reality. Inkscape provided a simple way to draw vector artwork for laser cutting. Rhino 3D's versatility made it ideal for translating those drawings into precise 3D models and testing their mechanical behavior. Ponoko's laser‑cutting service offered on‑demand manufacturing with a wide choice of materials and rapid turnaround, making it feasible to iterate and produce retail‑quality components without owning expensive equipment.

Cricut's ability to draw, score and cut paper or cardstock enabled small‑batch packaging development, allowing the creator to present Thing Y professionally during the pilot program. The provisional patent provided legal protection while the product was refined.

Potential and Future Opportunities

• Educational value: The toy encourages children and adults to experiment with geometry, magnetism and spatial reasoning. Building triangles, pyramids and other shapes introduces basic concepts of engineering and mathematics in a hands‑on way.

• Fidget & stress relief: The satisfying click of magnets and the ability to spin beams provide sensory stimulation, making Thing Y appealing as a desk toy or stress‑relief fidget.

• Customization: Because components are laser cut, future versions could explore different materials (wood, metal, colored acrylic) or engraved patterns. Ponoko's catalog of over 200 laser‑safe materials offers opportunities to tailor the toy's tactile feel and appearance.

• Modularity: Additional accessory parts—such as hubs, hinges or connector plates—could expand building possibilities. Parametric modeling in Rhino makes it straightforward to design and test these additions.

• Scale & distribution: The pilot's sell‑out indicates strong local demand. Scaling production through on‑demand services and partnering with additional retailers or online platforms could reach a broader audience.

Conclusion

Thing Y's journey from a sketch to a sold‑out product illustrates the power of rapid prototyping workflows. Hand drawings established the concept, Inkscape transformed sketches into vector artwork, and Rhino 3D enabled precise digital modeling. A provisional patent protected the idea while prototypes were refined using wooden rulers, 3D printing and laser‑cut acrylic produced through Ponoko's service. Custom packaging made with a Cricut Maker allowed professional presentation without large production runs. The pilot program at A2Z Science & Learning Store demonstrated market acceptance, with the medium and big sets selling out.

By combining digital precision with physical play, Thing Y captures the magic of turning an idea into a tangible object and points to a future where creative experimentation and accessible fabrication tools empower inventors to bring innovative toys to life.

"Test Tube Babies" - An Architectural Exploration in Vase Design

Overview
"Test Tube Babies" is a distinctive series of bud vases, conceived as both functional objects and sculptural explorations. These creations uniquely blend diverse materials such as hardwoods, aluminum sheet metal, Corian, colored plastics, and plexiglass. The resulting vases are elegant yet architectural, designed around the central concept of a simple test tube acting as a minimalist floral holder.

Conceptualization and Material Selection

The project's inception involved exploring contrasts between natural textures and industrial materials. Materials were selected based on visual appeal, structural properties, and the interplay between warmth (woods) and modernist coolness (metals, plastics). Each material's inherent qualities informed the design decisions, fostering a dialogue between organic and synthetic aesthetics.

Lamination and Fabrication Process

The foundational step involved the meticulous lamination of selected materials. This required careful preparation and precision gluing to ensure structural integrity and visual harmony. Hardwoods such as walnut, maple, and cherry were paired with aluminum sheets, translucent plexiglass, vividly colored plastics, and durable Corian to create visually compelling, multi‑layered blocks.

After curing, these laminated blocks underwent precision cutting into geometric forms, emphasizing clean lines and striking angles. Using tools like table saws, miter saws, and routers, each piece was crafted to highlight the intricate lamination patterns.

Architectural Cavities and Metal Embedding

To elevate the design further, specific pieces incorporated extruded aluminum elements, strategically embedded into the wood and composite materials. This embedding involved precision mortise cutting, ensuring tight, secure fits that accentuated the structural aesthetic of the design.

The resulting architectural cavities served both as visual focal points and as functional elements, contributing to the overall structural integrity and geometric complexity of each vase.

Final Detailing: Drilling for Functionality

The final stage of fabrication involved drilling precisely sized holes to snugly hold a single test tube, transforming each piece from a purely sculptural object into a functional bud vase. These vases found commercial success and were sold for a period at popular Northampton locations including Sticks and Bricks and Workroom Design Studio, gaining appreciation within the local artisan community. This minimalist floral presentation allowed each piece to maintain its sculptural integrity while serving its intended purpose.

Outcome and Reception

"Test Tube Babies" were celebrated for their innovative blending of art, architecture, and practical design. The juxtaposition of materials and clean, architectural forms resonated strongly with enthusiasts of contemporary design and craftsmanship. These vases successfully demonstrated how meticulous attention to materials, precision crafting techniques, and innovative design could yield objects that are both aesthetically pleasing and practically functional.

The resulting collection underscores the potential of cross‑disciplinary design approaches, highlighting how material experimentation can elevate everyday objects into sculptural art.

You love your dog more than most humans, but you're tired of playing doorman every time they want to explore the backyard or come back inside—and the commercial pet doors either look terrible, don't fit your specific setup, or cost more than a small appliance. This dog door project was born from the simple recognition that sometimes the best solutions to everyday problems are the ones you design and build yourself.

That's where Knectar's practical making approach led to creating what's essentially a custom access solution—combining traditional woodworking skills with CNC precision to design and fabricate a dog door that could be perfectly sized for a specific pet, seamlessly integrated into existing architecture, and built to last decades rather than seasons. The project explored how thoughtful design and quality construction could turn a simple functional need into an opportunity for craftsmanship.

The magic was in discovering how many design decisions go into something as seemingly simple as a dog door: the right height and width for comfortable passage, the proper spring tension for easy opening but secure closing, weather sealing that actually works, mounting solutions that don't compromise structural integrity, and finishes that complement rather than clash with existing home design.

The transformation created a custom solution that solved a specific problem while honoring both function and aesthetics. Sometimes the best design projects are the smallest ones—solutions that make daily life just a little bit easier while demonstrating that good design, quality materials, and careful construction can elevate even the most humble functional objects into something worth taking pride in.
